title: The whirling disc of NGC 4526
caption: The lenticular galaxy NGC 4526, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Dark lanes of dust and a bright, diffuse glow make NGC 4526 look like a halo hanging in empty space. The calm appearance is misleading. Among lenticular galaxies, a type that sits somewhere between spirals and ellipticals, NGC 4526 is one of the brightest known.

At its center is a supermassive black hole with the mass of 450 million Suns. The galaxy has also hosted two known supernovae, one in 1969 and one in 1994. It belongs to the Virgo cluster of galaxies, where observations from the ground have shown that a quarter of the galaxies seem to have fast-spinning discs of gas at their centers.

NGC 4526 has the most impressive of these. Its disc of gas, dust and stars stretches unusually far from the center, spanning some 7% of the galaxy's whole radius, and it spins at more than 250 kilometers per second. Astronomers used the motion of this disc to work out the mass of the central black hole, a method never before used for that purpose.

understand.summary: Hubble observed NGC 4526 in visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Some filters record near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the galaxy's dust lanes would not be visible to the unaided eye.

explore: The picture was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. Judy Schmidt entered a version of it into the Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition, which invited enthusiasts to search the Hubble archive for images the public had never seen.
